**TrueLayer raises €23m with Italian state backing for pay-by-bank expansion**

*Italian state interest in building domestic open banking infrastructure is signalled by CDP Venture Capital's lead investment as TrueLayer prepares to scale in its founders' home market.*

TrueLayer has raised €23 million in a funding round led by CDP Venture Capital, the venture arm of Italy's state-owned development bank Cassa Depositi e Prestiti. The round will support the company's expansion into Italy alongside continued growth in the UK and wider Europe.

The identity of the lead investor is as significant as the amount. CDP Venture Capital is an instrument of Italian industrial policy; its participation positions pay-by-bank as part of Italy's broader push to modernise domestic payment infrastructure. TrueLayer was founded in London in 2016 by Italians Francesco Simoneschi and Luca Martinetti, and Italy represents a large, underpenetrated market for account-to-account payments.

The raise comes after an active period for TrueLayer, which acquired Dutch BNPL firm Pelai and launched its bank-on-file product to challenge card-on-file at checkout. The company has also partnered with SumUp on open banking account top-ups. With Mollie's completion of the GoCardless acquisition in September, the European pay-by-bank landscape is consolidating around a smaller number of well-capitalised players.

**Mastercard to mandate offline payment capability across Europe from 2027**

*Addressing growing concerns about digital payment resilience, the mandate will require terminals to process transactions during power and network outages from 2027.*

Mastercard is introducing offline payment requirements across Europe that will take effect from 2027, enabling consumers to complete card transactions during power cuts and network failures. The mandate will require terminals to process payments without a live connection, storing them for later settlement.

The move responds directly to concerns that have intensified as cash usage declines. Several European countries have experienced payment disruptions during outages, most recently the Worldpay failure during a World Cup match in June. As card and digital payments become the default, the absence of a fallback mechanism becomes a systemic risk rather than an inconvenience. The European Central Bank and national central banks have repeatedly flagged payment resilience as a policy priority, and the digital euro proposal includes an offline capability for the same reason.

Mastercard's decision to impose the requirement through its own network rules, rather than waiting for regulation, gives it a first-mover position on an issue that legislators are likely to address eventually. It also adds a practical differentiator at a time when both card schemes face increasing competitive pressure from account-to-account alternatives and the growing Wero network.

*Sources: [Mastercard to enable offline payments across Europe](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48560/mastercard-to-enable-offline-payments-across-europe?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**FCA taskforce maps open finance use cases and identifies infrastructure gaps**

*Governance and operating model choices matter as much as technical capability in scaling open finance beyond payments, according to the PRISM taskforce's findings.*

The Financial Conduct Authority's PRISM taskforce has published findings from its assessment of open finance use cases, concluding that common infrastructure, governance and operating model choices are as important as the individual applications they support. The taskforce examined how open finance principles could extend beyond payment accounts into areas such as mortgages, pensions and insurance.

The publication sits alongside a separate FCA report summarising outputs from its mortgages and open finance policy sprint, which examined how open finance data could reshape mortgage affordability assessments. Together, the documents advance the FCA's open finance roadmap, published in April, by identifying specific barriers to adoption and areas where regulatory intervention or industry coordination may be needed.

The emphasis on shared infrastructure and governance echoes a recurring theme in European open finance discussions: that technical connectivity alone is insufficient without agreed standards for data quality, liability and consumer consent. The FCA's approach contrasts with the EU's Financial Data Access regulation, which takes a more prescriptive legislative route to similar ends.

*Sources: [FCA's PRISM Taskforce publishes Open Finance use case impact findings](https://www.openbankingexpo.com/news/fcas-prism-taskforce-publishes-open-finance-use-case-impact-findings/) — Openbankingexpo | [Open finance and the future of mortgage lending: FCA sprint outcomes for the industry](https://www.addleshawgoddard.com/en/insights/insights-briefings/2026/financial-regulation/financial-regulation-in-the-know-consumer-finance-october-2026/open-finance-future-mortgage-lending-fca-sprint-outcomes-industry/) — Addleshawgoddard*

**Visa and Mastercard face £700m claim over post-Brexit interchange fee rises**

*A new legal challenge argues that interchange fee increases on transactions between UK merchants and EEA-issued cards after Brexit were unjustified and anticompetitive.*

Visa and Mastercard are facing a £700 million legal claim over their decision to increase interchange fees on transactions between UK businesses and EEA-issued cards following Brexit. The claim argues that the fee increases, which took effect after the UK lost the protection of the EU's Interchange Fee Regulation, were unjustified and anticompetitive.

The Payment Systems Regulator found that Visa and Mastercard account for nine in 10 online transactions at UK businesses using EEA-issued cards, giving them substantial pricing power in the absence of the EU cap. Both schemes raised cross-border interchange fees after Brexit, with some rates increasing several-fold. The PSR's earlier market review into scheme fees, and its May proposal to require mandatory profit reporting from both networks, form the regulatory backdrop to this litigation.

The claim adds legal risk to the commercial and regulatory pressure already bearing on the card schemes' UK fee structures. It arrives as alternative payment methods, including the newly launched UK Payments Initiative and growing pay-by-bank adoption, offer merchants potential routes to reduce card dependency.

*Sources: [Visa and Mastercard face £700 million claim over post-Brexit card fees](https://iclg.com/news/visa-and-mastercard-face-700-million-claim-over-post-brexit-card-fees/) — ICLG*

**FCA's David Geale outlines position on crypto rules, agentic AI liability and open finance**

*Sets out how the regulator is approaching the convergence of crypto, AI agents and open finance across several policy fronts simultaneously.*

David Geale, the FCA's executive director of payments and digital finance, has outlined the regulator's thinking on several converging fronts in an interview with FinTech Futures. Geale addressed the FCA's approach to crypto asset regulation, the question of liability when AI agents initiate payments, and the path toward open finance in the UK.

On agentic AI, Geale acknowledged that existing regulatory frameworks do not cleanly address scenarios where autonomous agents make financial decisions on behalf of consumers. The question of who bears liability when an AI agent initiates a payment that goes wrong remains unresolved, and the FCA is examining how its rules might need to adapt. The regulator published its AI review in July with agentic payments explicitly in scope.

Geale's comments on open finance reinforced the FCA's incremental approach, contrasting the UK's market-led model with the EU's legislative route through the Financial Data Access regulation. He pointed to progress made since roughly 2023, when none of these issues were on the regulatory agenda.

"No open banking, no open finance, no tokenised deposits, no stablecoins," he said, framing the current moment as one of rapid convergence requiring careful but responsive oversight.

*Sources: [Interview: The FCA's David Geale on crypto rules, agentic AI liability, and open finance](https://www.fintechfutures.com/regulations-compliance/interview-the-fcas-david-geale-on-crypto-rules-agentic-ai-liability-and-open-finance) — Fintechfutures*
